title: What Is a Personal CRM? Comparing 6 Types of Contact Systems
summary: What is a personal CRM? Software that tracks who you know, when you last spoke and when to follow up. Compare 6 options, from spreadsheets to dedicated apps.
body_markdown:
A personal CRM (sometimes called a PRM, or "personal relationship manager") is software that stores your personal and professional contacts alongside a running history of when you talked, what you talked about, and when you're due to reach out again. The core job it does that a phone[contacts app or any other contact management system](https://getdex.com/blog/contact-management-software/) doesn't: it surfaces *who you're losing touch with* instead of just storing a name and number.


That single feature (automated follow-up surfacing) is the line that separates a good personal CRM from the five other ways people already manage contacts: the native address book, a spreadsheet, a DIY Notion or Airtable database, a repurposed business CRM, and a dedicated personal CRM app (either cloud-hosted or self-hosted open source). Below is how those six actually compare, not just in features but in what breaks first as your network grows.


## Fast Facts about a Personal CRM


-


**Free tier that already works for most people:** your phone's native contacts app (Google/Apple/Outlook Contacts). It costs nothing and needs no setup, but it has no reminders and no interaction log.


-


**Where spreadsheets break:** past roughly 40-60 tracked contacts, follow-ups only happen if you remember to open the file. There's no system-generated nudge.


-


**Cheapest system with a real reminder engine:**[Monica](https://www.monicahq.com/) , open source and free to self-host on your own server, or $9 a month ($90 a year) for the hosted version.


-


**Dedicated apps, priced as of October 2026:** Dex ([$12 a month for Premium, $20 for Professional](https://getdex.com/pricing/?ref=blog&ref_post=what-is-a-personal-crm) , billed annually, with a 7-day free trial),[Folk](https://www.folk.app/) (from $24 per member a month, billed annually), and[Cloze](https://www.cloze.com/) ($17 a month, billed annually). All three cost more on month-to-month billing.


-


**Watch out:** older "best personal CRM" roundups still recommend Clay. That app was renamed[Mesh](https://me.sh/) in March 2026. Don't confuse it with[clay.com](https://www.clay.com/) , an unrelated data platform for sales teams.

## Native Address Book: Why It's Still the Right Call for Most People


For anyone tracking fewer than about 50 people they actually want to stay in touch with, the contacts app already on your phone does the job. It syncs across devices, backs up automatically with your account, and requires no setup. What it can't do is remind you that you haven't talked to someone in four months. That's a manual job, every time, and it's the exact gap every other system on this list exists to close.


## Spreadsheets: Where the Wheels Come Off


A spreadsheet gives you one row per person and whatever columns you decide to add, such as last contacted date, notes, and tags. It works well until the row count climbs into the 40-60 range, at which point two things happen at once: sorting by "last contacted" stops being a habit you remember to do, and the notes column becomes a wall of text nobody re-reads before a call. The spreadsheet itself never breaks; the habit of checking it does. That's the mechanism every dedicated CRM below is built to replace with a system-generated nudge instead of a self-imposed one.


## Notion and Airtable: Structure Without Sync


A[Notion](https://www.notion.com/) or[Airtable](https://airtable.com/) personal CRM template gives you relational databases, saved views (board, calendar, timeline), and tags. That's a real upgrade over a flat spreadsheet for organizing the information. What it doesn't give you is contact sync: your actual phone numbers and emails still live in your phone's contacts or your email client, and nothing in Notion pulls a new LinkedIn message or a calendar meeting into the record automatically. You're building a better filing cabinet, not an automated one.

## Self-Hosted Open Source: Monica


Monica is the DIY option for anyone who wants the full personal-CRM feature set (reminders, interaction timelines, notes, tags) without a vendor holding the data. Free if you run it on your own server; a managed hosted version exists for people who want the software without the sysadmin work. The tradeoff is direct: you (or your setup) own uptime, backups, and version updates. There's no support line to call if something breaks at 11pm.


> [Read Dex vs. Monica Here](https://getdex.com/blog/dex-vs-monica)


## Dedicated Personal CRM Apps: Dex, Folk, Cloze


This is the category most "best personal CRM" listicles are actually reviewing. These apps add a browser extension or email/calendar integration that auto-captures contact context (a LinkedIn connection, a Gmail thread, a calendar invite) and turns it into a contact record or timeline entry without manual typing. Dex leans toward LinkedIn-heavy networkers, with connection sync, job titles that update on their own, and research briefings on a contact; Folk and Cloze compete on broader integrations (email, calendar, sometimes social). The recurring cost buys automation. It also means your relationship notes live on someone else's servers.


**Two recent changes worth flagging:** UpHabit shut down its personal CRM apps on April 9, 2026. And Clay, still cited in a lot of 2023-2024-era "best personal CRM" content, was renamed Mesh in March 2026. It is still a personal CRM, with a free plan for up to 1,000 contacts, and we cover it in[Dex vs Clay (Mesh)](https://getdex.com/blog/dex-vs-clay/) . The old name now causes confusion because clay.com belongs to a different company, which sells a go-to-market data platform to sales teams. If a "best personal CRM" list from that period is your only source, check that each product still exists under that name before you sign up.


## Repurposed Business CRMs


If you already run[HubSpot's free CRM](https://www.hubspot.com/products/crm) or a[monday.com CRM](https://monday.com/crm) for freelance client work, it's tempting to just add your personal contacts into the same tool instead of paying for a second app. It works, technically. But these tools are built around deal stages and pipelines, and a "Grandma's birthday" entry sitting next to a sales pipeline stage is a UI mismatch you'll feel every time you open it. Fine as a stopgap, not a long-term fit.

## Where Dex comes in


[Dex](https://getdex.com/) is one of the dedicated apps compared above. It is also our product, so read this section with that in mind. It does the three things this article keeps returning to. It pulls people and context in automatically from Gmail, Outlook, Google Calendar, LinkedIn, WhatsApp and, in beta, iMessage (see[the full list of integrations](https://getdex.com/integrations/) ). It has a keep-in-touch reminder engine: you set how often you want to be in contact with someone, and Dex resurfaces them when that time is up. And it keeps a timeline for each person, so your notes, meetings and latest messages are in one place when you sit down to write to them.


By the break-even table above, that is worth paying for once you're past 150 people and can no longer say from memory who you last spoke to. Below that, your phone's contacts app or a spreadsheet usually still holds, and a subscription you stop opening helps nobody. If you're past that point and still deciding between the paid options, our[guide to choosing a personal CRM](https://getdex.com/guides/best-personal-crm/) goes through them in more depth. If you already know that auto-capture and reminders are what you're missing,[try Dex free for 7 days](https://getdex.com/preboard/?ref=blog&ref_post=what-is-a-personal-crm) .


## Who this isn't for


-


**You track fewer than 30-40 people you actually want to stay in touch with.** A paid personal CRM is a subscription for a problem your phone's contacts app already solves. It won't get used past week two.


-


**You want zero vendor access to your relationship notes.** Skip cloud SaaS options (Dex, Folk, Cloze) and use a spreadsheet or self-hosted Monica instead. Your notes about people stay on hardware you control.


-


**You already pay for a business CRM and your "personal" contacts are mostly client-adjacent.** Adding a second, separate personal CRM app just means updating two systems for overlapping people. Use one.


-


**You want a complete archive of your text messages.** Dex syncs WhatsApp and, in a beta for Mac, iMessage and SMS. For each contact it updates the last-contact date and shows the most recent message. It does not store the full conversation. Cloze lists text message syncing among its features, and Folk lists WhatsApp sync. If you need every message captured and searchable, check exactly what a tool stores before you pay for it.


## Original Research: Cross-Referencing 7 Tools' Public Pricing and Feature Pages


To build the break-even matrix above, we cross-referenced the publicly listed feature pages and pricing tiers of seven contact-management options (Google Contacts, a Google Sheets template, a Notion template, Monica, Dex, Mesh, and Folk) as of October 2026, mapping each one against two variables: whether it auto-captures interaction data (versus requiring manual entry) and whether it has a system-generated follow-up reminder at all. Only three of the seven (Dex, Folk, Mesh) combine both auto-capture and reminders. Monica has the reminders but depends on manual entry. The Clay rename stood out as a gap in current comparison content: many roundups, including ones dated 2026, still list the app under its old name, and clay.com is a separate company that sells to sales teams. A solo reader who follows the old name ends up evaluating the wrong product.


---


## Frequently Asked Questions


**Is a personal CRM worth it?**


It's worth it once you're tracking more people than you can reliably remember to follow up with manually, typically somewhere past 50-150 contacts, based on the break-even matrix above. Below that, a native address book or spreadsheet covers the same ground for free.


**What's the difference between a personal CRM and a business CRM?**


Business CRMs (Salesforce, HubSpot) are built around deal stages, pipelines, and team reporting for one company selling to many customers. A personal CRM is built for one person managing many individual relationships over time, with no sales-stage structure at all.


**Can I use Notion as a personal CRM?**


Yes, for structure. Tags, saved views, and relational databases work well. It[won't auto-capture calendar invites, emails, or texts](https://getdex.com/blog/notion-vs-dex/) the way dedicated apps like Dex or Folk do; you're still typing in every interaction by hand.


**Is Google Contacts a personal CRM?**


No. It's an address book. It stores names, numbers, and emails but has[no interaction timeline and no follow-up reminder engine](https://getdex.com/blog/dex-vs-google-contacts/) , which is the defining feature of a personal CRM.


**What's the best free personal CRM?**


Monica, self-hosted, is the most feature-complete free option, with full reminders and timelines and no subscription, if you're willing to run your own server. For zero setup, a Notion template or your phone's native contacts app are the free alternatives. Mesh, the app formerly called Clay, also has a free plan for up to 1,000 contacts.


## Bottom Line


Start with what you already have. If your phone's contacts app or a spreadsheet is starting to fail you (meaning you're forgetting to follow up, not just that the UI feels dated), move to a system with an actual reminder engine: Monica if you want to self-host for free, Dex or Folk if you'd rather pay for auto-capture and skip the setup. If an older list sent you looking for Clay, the personal CRM is now called Mesh, and clay.com is a different company's sales tool. And don't add a second CRM on top of a business CRM you already pay for.
